title: Case study: water supply in Windhoek, Namibia

blocks.heading: The case study: water supply in Windhoek
blocks.text: How one of the driest capitals in southern Africa supplies its people, and how it manages a scarce resource.

blocks.heading: Windhoek: the supply
blocks.text: Windhoek, Namibia's capital, supplies about 450 000 people (mid-2010s, rounded) on the Central Plateau, one of the driest parts of the country, with roughly 300-400 millimetres of rain a year, nearly all in summer. The sources are several: boreholes into aquifers beneath and beside the city; the Goreangab and Avis dams on small seasonal rivers, which fill in the wet months and stand low after dry ones; and the direct re-use plant, which treats the city's waste water and returns it to the drinking taps - the oldest such plant in continuous use worldwide, running since the late 1960s. The sources are told apart by how their water travels: pumped from the aquifer, drawn from the dam, or cycled from the city's own drains.

blocks.heading: The management, step by step
blocks.text: The water is managed in steps. Tariffs rise with use, so the more a household consumes, the more each litre costs - in the drought year of 2016 these tariffs were central to cutting the city's consumption sharply. The re-use plant recycles waste water, so a litre drawn once serves the city twice, which stretches every borehole and dam. And the boreholes are pumped within measured limits, so the aquifers are drawn down slowly and recover in wetter years. The city also stores water in aquifers on purpose, recharging them in wet seasons. Together the steps show management as the condition of supply: a desert capital keeps its taps through metering, recycling and restraint, and every strategy names something specific - a tariff, a plant, a pumping limit - rather than an abstraction.
